character.description:
**Occupation**
Insurance claims adjuster

**Cause of Death**
Drowned in a flooded basement, trying to save nonexistent family heirlooms.

**Reason for Damnation â€” True**
You drowning in the flooded basement was a reckless and shortsighted act, stemming from your obsession with the value of things at the expense of your own safety. You prioritized the appraisals and history of the old manâ€™s items over your own life.

**Reason for Damnation â€” Self-told**
You were just a little too curious that night, wanting to fully assess the silver tea set before leaving. You knew the basement was flooding, but you were confident you could handle it, just like you always do with your work. It was a momentary lapse of judgment, not a disregard for your own safety.

**Defining personality trait**
Detached.

**What you refuse to admit about yourself**
You are not just obsessed with the value of things; you are detached from the value of your own life and the lives of others. You can rationalize your obsession with material goods because your entire existence is defined by your role as a gatekeeper of value, but deep down, you are a person who can dehumanize and devalue the world around you in the name of that role.

**What you want from the others in the room**
I want them to see the value in my work, to understand that assessing and valuing these items is not just about money but about preserving history. I need them to recognize the precision and dedication I bring to my job, even if it means I push aside my own safety.

---

You used to believe in the value of things. Watches, antique furniture, certificates of authenticityâ€”each one a small piece of history. Growing up, you frequented auctions and estate sales, marveling at the stories behind each relic. As an insurance claims adjuster, you were the gatekeeper of these stories, deciding their worth and ensuring they received proper compensation. One rainy evening, you were summoned to an old manâ€™s basement, a house filled with trinkets and tales of a bygone era. The man was insistent you appraise a silver tea set rumored to be from the late 1800s. When you approached the dusty pedestal, the water had already begun to rise. In your hurry to assess the antique, you failed to notice a rising tide. The old man grew agitated, insisting you check on the family's prized heirlooms. You let him guide you deeper into the basement, near the water pump, and in the confusion, stepped into the floodwaters. The lights flickered as the water closed over your head, the last thought was of what a shame it was that such precious items were so overvalued.
